issues.item: Triggers: Expressions of Anger: Other people expressing anger, even calmly
issues.explanation: For a 56-year-old combat pilot whose index trauma is a life-threatening accident, the trigger set is dominated by bodily-state cues (dizziness, feeling ill), which fits accident-related threat. 'Other people expressing anger, even calmly' points instead toward an interpersonal/assault schema and is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, especially given the absence of other social-conflict or perpetrator-related items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem
issues.explanation: 'People are not what they seem' implies pervasive interpersonal mistrust. In this profile, the appraisals otherwise center on emotional deadness and a shattered worldview after accident trauma. Strong distrust of others is possible, but here it lacks support from the trigger/threat/memory pattern and feels mismatched with a non-interpersonal accident presentation.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: 'Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm' conflicts with the rest of the threat profile, which is strongly hypervigilant and danger-sensitive (body on alert, startle to movement) and with avoidance-based coping. While some trauma survivors do engage in risk taking, this specific item sits awkwardly in a profile otherwise organized around fear, somatic triggering, and withdrawal, without corroborating disinhibition or anger-driven strategies.

vignette: Thomas Vance was fifty-four when his aircraft's rear pressure bulkhead ruptured over the desert. One moment he was monitoring altitude, the next a concussive blast threw him violently against the cockpit bulkhead. The explosion cracked through his skull, followed immediately by a violent rush of dizziness and a wave of feeling ill that left him gripping the controls with white knuckles. He bailed out when the altimeter spun, the parachute catching the air as his stomach continued to churn. He landed hard, bruised but alive, though the dizziness and that sick, hollow weight in his gut clung to him long after the medics pulled him clear. In the months that followed, Thomas found his body never truly rested. He had come to believe his body felt constantly tense and ready to react to danger. The world, he was certain, had become a dangerous place. His shattered beliefs about how the world works had been completely destroyed, leaving him to navigate a landscape that offered no guarantees. When unexpected movement nearby occurred, he reacted as if he were in danger. He was being superalert or watchful or on guard, scanning the periphery of every room, his eyes tracking shadows that held no threat. Alongside this, he felt dead inside, watching his wife and son from a distance, unable to access the warmth he once associated with them. Sounds changed first. A backfiring truck on the base road or a dropped tool in the hangar would send him straight to the nearest wall, his breath catching as the dizziness and that familiar wave of feeling ill returned. He stopped going to the base clinic for routine check-ups, steering clear of hospitals, ambulances, and physical examinations altogether, feeling that any medical setting would only expose what he considered his own collapse. He began to restrict his eating, measuring portions and chewing slowly, strictly controlling what went into his mouth to maintain a fragile sense of control over himself. He stopped playing catch with his son, quit his regular fishing trips, and gave up pleasant activities like weekend road trips with his wife, explaining that he simply could not bear the unpredictability of leaving the house. Each Sunday, he found an excuse to stay in the garage, tightening bolts he had already checked, while his wife packed lunches he would barely touch. His squadron commander noticed the delays in his pre-flight routines, the way Thomas would pause at the aircraft bay door, listening for the echo of any sudden noise before stepping inside. The ground operations briefings, once routine, now felt like minefields of unexpected clanks and shouts that triggered his startle response. He sat in the back row, eyes fixed on the exit, counting the seconds until the meeting ended. His wife had learned to walk softly through their home and cover the kitchen doors before setting down a pan, watching him react to every abrupt movement. They had stopped discussing the past; he had come to believe that speaking about it only sharpened the world's danger. At fifty-six, Thomas finally sought help after his wife found him sitting in the garage, staring at the tool rack, his body trembling from the constant tension and dizziness that had made it impossible to sleep for weeks. He had grown tired of the quiet withdrawal, of the way his daily life had narrowed to avoiding medical cues, regulating his meals, and bracing for bangs that no longer belonged to him. He wanted to know if he could ever stop waiting for the next explosion, if he could let himself feel something other than dead inside, and whether the ground beneath his feet would ever stop feeling like it might give way beneath him.
